items.title: The 1991 Crisis and the LPG Reforms
items.body:
## In one line

In 1991 India nearly ran out of foreign money to pay for imports, and the rescue reshaped the whole economy through the **LPG reforms**. Asked for the crisis cause, the gold pledge and who led the reforms.

## Why the crisis happened

By 1991 India faced a severe **balance of payments crisis**:

- **Foreign exchange reserves** had fallen to about **US$1.2 billion — barely 2–3 weeks of import cover**.
- **Twin deficits**: large fiscal deficit and current-account/trade deficit; ballooning **external debt**.
- **Trigger**: the **Gulf War (1990–91)** spiked oil prices and cut remittances from the Gulf.

## The response

- India pledged **gold** to raise forex (RBI airlifted ~47 tonnes to the Bank of England; ~20 tonnes to UBS) and secured an **IMF bailout**.
- PM **P.V. Narasimha Rao** and FM **Dr. Manmohan Singh** launched the **LPG reforms** (New Economic Policy).

## LPG = Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation

| Pillar | Core idea |
|---|---|
| **Liberalisation** | Free market forces — abolish industrial licensing, cut controls |
| **Privatisation** | Reduce state's role — disinvest in PSEs |
| **Globalisation** | Integrate with world economy — trade, FDI, FTAs |

**Trade-strategy shift:** before 1991 India followed **import substitution** (make at home what you import, behind high tariffs and quotas). Globalisation moved it to **export promotion and global integration** — lower tariffs, removal of quantitative restrictions, FDI and SEZs.

Reforms are also grouped as **stabilisation** (short-term BoP/inflation correction) and **structural** (long-term efficiency-raising) measures.

**Don't confuse:** India pledged gold and took an IMF loan precisely so that it would **not default** — India never defaulted on its external debt in 1991.

## Terms explained

- **Balance of payments (BoP) crisis** — when a country cannot pay for its imports or debts in foreign currency.
- **Import cover** — how many weeks of imports the forex reserves can pay for (1991: just 2–3 weeks).
- **LPG** — Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation.
- **IMF bailout** — emergency loan from the International Monetary Fund, with reform conditions.

## TL;DR

- 1991 forex reserves fell to ~US$1.2 bn, about 2–3 weeks of import cover, triggering a BoP crisis.
- Causes: high fiscal/trade deficits, rising external debt, Gulf-War oil-price spike and falling remittances.
- India pledged gold (RBI airlifted ~47 t to Bank of England) and took an IMF bailout.
- LPG reforms launched by PM P.V. Narasimha Rao and FM Dr. Manmohan Singh (1991).
- LPG = Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation; also framed as stabilisation vs structural reforms.

items.title: Key Reform Measures (Industry, Trade, Finance)
items.body:
## In one line

This note lists the **concrete steps** of the 1991 reforms across industry, trade and finance — delicensing, disinvestment, SEBI and SEZs. Asked for which controls were removed and when.

## Liberalisation measures

- **Abolition of industrial licensing** for most industries (except a few strategic/security sectors).
- **MRTP Act amended (1991)** — later replaced by the **Competition Act, 2002**.
- **De-reservation** of sectors earlier reserved for the public sector.

## Privatisation

- **Disinvestment**: sale of government equity in PSEs via IPO/offer-for-sale (minority stake) or **strategic sale** (transfer of control).
- **Department of Disinvestment created in 1999**; landmark strategic sales — **BALCO, VSNL**.

## Trade & financial reforms

- **Tariff cuts and removal of quantitative restrictions**; **Special Economic Zones (SEZs)** to boost exports.
- **SEBI established in 1992** as capital-market regulator.
- **Narasimham Committee** reforms in banking — cut in **SLR/CRR**, Basel norms, more competition.
- Later steps: **GST (2017)**, faceless assessment, four **Labour Codes (2019–20)**.

## Terms explained

- **Industrial licensing** — the old permit system a firm needed before producing (mostly abolished in 1991).
- **Disinvestment** — the government selling part of its stake in a public-sector company.
- **Strategic sale** — selling a controlling stake so management passes to a private buyer.
- **SEZ** — Special Economic Zone: an export enclave with tax and customs benefits.

## TL;DR

- Industrial licensing abolished for most industries; only a few strategic sectors retained licences.
- MRTP Act amended (1991), later replaced by the Competition Act, 2002.
- Disinvestment = sale of government stake in PSEs; Department of Disinvestment set up in 1999 (BALCO, VSNL sold).
- Trade reforms: tariff cuts, removal of quantitative restrictions, and Special Economic Zones (SEZs).
- SEBI established in 1992; Narasimham Committee guided banking reforms (SLR/CRR cuts, Basel norms).

items.title: Balance of Payments — Structure & Convertibility
items.body:
## In one line

The **Balance of Payments** is the country's full account of money coming in and going out across its borders. Asked for its three sub-accounts and the current-vs-capital convertibility distinction.

## What the BoP is

The **Balance of Payments** records **all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world** over a period, on a **double-entry** basis. In accounting terms the **overall BoP always balances**; a 'deficit' or 'surplus' refers to a sub-account.

## Three accounts

| Account | What it records |
|---|---|
| **Current** | Merchandise trade, services, income, unilateral transfers (remittances, aid) |
| **Capital** | Capital transfers (debt forgiveness), non-produced non-financial assets (patents) |
| **Financial** | FDI, portfolio investment, reserve assets (forex, gold, SDRs) |

*(An 'Errors and Omissions' entry reconciles data gaps.)*

## Rupee convertibility

- **Current-account convertibility since August 1994** (India accepted IMF Article VIII) — free forex for trade, travel, remittances.
- **Capital-account convertibility is only partial/calibrated**; the **Tarapore Committees (1997, 2006)** gave a phased roadmap.

## Correcting a BoP problem

Export promotion, import substitution, building forex reserves, and prudent fiscal/monetary policy.

## Terms explained

- **Current account** — day-to-day flows: trade in goods, services, income and remittances.
- **Capital & financial account** — investment flows: FDI, portfolio money, loans, reserves.
- **Convertibility** — the freedom to exchange rupees for foreign currency.
- **Double-entry** — every transaction is booked twice (a credit and a debit), so the total always balances.

## TL;DR

- BoP = double-entry record of all transactions between residents and the rest of the world; overall account always balances.
- Current account: merchandise, services, income, unilateral transfers.
- Capital account: capital transfers and non-produced non-financial assets; Financial account: FDI, portfolio, reserve assets.
- Rupee is convertible on current account since August 1994 (IMF Article VIII).
- Capital-account convertibility remains partial; Tarapore Committees (1997, 2006) gave the roadmap.

items.title: FDI vs FPI vs FII, Routes & Sectoral Caps
items.body:
## In one line

This note explains the difference between **foreign money that builds factories (FDI)** and **foreign money that just buys shares (FPI/FII)**, plus who regulates each and the sector caps. A frequent prelims confusion-pair.

## The three foreign-investment types

| Feature | FDI | FPI / FII |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Long-term, in productive assets | Short-term, in financial assets |
| Control | Control/influence over the company | No management control (passive) |
| Volatility | Stable | Volatile ('hot money') |
| Regulator | DPIIT (policy), RBI (FEMA) | SEBI |

*FII is now merged into the broader **FPI** category under SEBI's FPI Regulations, 2019.*

## Framework & routes

- **FEMA, 1999** (replaced FERA 1973) governs foreign exchange; **DPIIT** (Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, under the **Ministry of Commerce and Industry**) frames FDI policy.
- Two entry routes: **Automatic** (no prior approval) and **Government/approval** route.
- The **FIPB was abolished in 2017**.

## Sectoral FDI caps (recent)

| Sector | Cap |
|---|---|
| Insurance | **100%** (Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha Act, December 2025; earlier 26% → 49% in 2014 → 74% in 2021) |
| Defence | 74% automatic (up to 100% by approval) |
| Telecom | 100% |
| Single-brand retail | 100% automatic |

**Don't confuse:** defence is **74%** automatic, while insurance moved from 74% to **100%** in December 2025; telecom and single-brand retail allow **100%**. No sector in this table is capped at 49% or 51% any more.

## Recent trend

Per the **Economic Survey 2023-24**, net FDI fell from **~US$42 bn (FY23) to ~US$26.5 bn (FY24)**; **digital FDI** rose sharply (share 46.6% in FY17 → 69.2% in FY21). Top sources: **Singapore, USA, Mauritius**.

## Terms explained

- **FDI** — Foreign Direct Investment: long-term money that buys/builds productive assets and gives control.
- **FPI / FII** — Foreign Portfolio/Institutional Investment: passive money in shares and bonds, easily withdrawn.
- **FEMA, 1999** — the law governing foreign-exchange dealings (replaced FERA).
- **Automatic vs Government route** — FDI needing no prior approval vs FDI needing approval.

## TL;DR

- FDI = long-term, control, DPIIT/RBI; FPI/FII = short-term, no control, volatile, regulated by SEBI.
- FEMA 1999 (replaced FERA 1973) governs forex; entry via Automatic or Government route; FIPB abolished 2017.
- FDI caps: insurance 100% (Dec 2025), defence 74% automatic, telecom 100%, single-brand retail 100%.
- Net FDI fell from ~US$42 bn (FY23) to ~US$26.5 bn (FY24) per Economic Survey 2023-24.
- Digital FDI share rose from 46.6% (FY17) to 69.2% (FY21); top sources Singapore, USA, Mauritius.

items.title: WTO — Structure, Principles & Agreements
items.body:
## In one line

The **World Trade Organization** writes and enforces the rules of global trade; India is a founding member. Asked for its year, principles (MFN, National Treatment) and the main agreements.

## Basics

- The **WTO** was established on **1 January 1995** under the **Marrakesh Agreement (1994)**, succeeding the **GATT** (in force since 1948).
- **HQ: Geneva**; **166 members** (as of 2024); **India is a founding member**; decisions largely by **consensus**.

## Core principles

- **Most-Favoured-Nation (MFN)** — a trade advantage given to one member must be extended to **all** members (no discrimination *between* partners).
- **National Treatment** — imported and domestic goods must be treated **equally** once in the market.

## Major agreements

| Agreement | Subject |
|---|---|
| **AoA** | Agriculture — market access, domestic support, export subsidies |
| **TRIPS** | Intellectual property rights |
| **TRIMS** | Trade-related investment measures |
| **GATS** | Trade in services |
| **SPS** | Sanitary & phytosanitary (food safety, plant/animal health) |

## India's stance

- Defends **public stockholding for food security** (MSP procurement) against AoA subsidy limits.
- Secured the **Peace Clause** at the **Bali Ministerial (2013)** — interim protection until a permanent solution.
- Pushes for lower agri-subsidy pressure on developing countries; the dispute-settlement Appellate Body is currently non-functional.

## Terms explained

- **WTO** — World Trade Organization: the global body that frames and enforces trade rules.
- **GATT** — the earlier General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (1948) that the WTO replaced.
- **MFN (Most-Favoured-Nation)** — a benefit given to one member must go to all members.
- **National Treatment** — foreign and domestic goods are treated equally once imported.

## TL;DR

- WTO established 1 January 1995 (Marrakesh Agreement 1994), succeeding GATT; HQ Geneva; 166 members.
- MFN = no discrimination between trading partners; National Treatment = equal treatment of foreign and domestic goods.
- Key agreements: AoA (agriculture), TRIPS (IP), TRIMS (investment), GATS (services), SPS (health standards).
- India defends public food-stockholding/MSP against AoA subsidy limits.
- Peace Clause agreed at the Bali Ministerial (2013) gives interim protection to food-security stockholding.

items.title: Foreign Trade Policy 2023 & Recent FTAs
items.body:
## In one line

This note covers India's current **Foreign Trade Policy (2023)** and its latest **free-trade agreements** (UAE, Australia, EFTA, UK). High-frequency current affairs — know which deal is with whom and when it came into force.

## Foreign Trade Policy (FTP) 2023

- Came into effect **1 April 2023**; administered by the **Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT)**, Ministry of Commerce.
- **No fixed end date** — a **dynamic, open-ended** policy updated as needed (a break from the earlier 5-year policies).
- **Target: US$2 trillion in exports (goods + services) by 2030.**
- **Four pillars**: incentive-to-remission; export promotion through collaboration; ease of doing business & e-initiatives; emerging areas (**e-commerce exports, districts as export hubs**).
- Introduced **Towns of Export Excellence** and a one-time **amnesty** for export-obligation defaults.

## Recent Free Trade Agreements

| FTA | Partner | In force |
|---|---|---|
| **CEPA** | UAE | 1 May 2022 |
| **ECTA** | Australia | 29 Dec 2022 |
| **TEPA** | EFTA (Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein) | 1 Oct 2025 |
| **CETA** | United Kingdom | 15 Jul 2026 |

- **India–UK CETA**: negotiations concluded 6 May 2025, **signed 24 July 2025**, in force **15 July 2026** — the UK's biggest FTA since Brexit.
- **India–EFTA TEPA**: signed 10 March 2024; carries an **unprecedented US$100 billion investment pledge** over 15 years.
- India **withdrew from RCEP (2019)** over concerns about its trade deficit with China, import surges and dairy-sector protection.

## Terms explained

- **FTP** — Foreign Trade Policy: the government's framework of export-import rules.
- **DGFT** — Directorate General of Foreign Trade, which runs the FTP.
- **FTA** — Free Trade Agreement: a pact cutting tariffs between partner countries.
- **CEPA / ECTA / TEPA / CETA** — India's deals with the UAE / Australia / EFTA / UK.

## TL;DR

- FTP 2023 took effect 1 April 2023 under the DGFT; it is dynamic with no sunset date.
- FTP 2023 targets US$2 trillion of exports (goods + services) by 2030.
- India–UAE CEPA in force May 2022; India–Australia ECTA in force December 2022.
- India–EFTA TEPA (signed March 2024, in force Oct 2025) carries a US$100 bn investment pledge over 15 years.
- India–UK CETA signed 24 July 2025, in force 15 July 2026; India withdrew from RCEP in 2019.

items.title: 1991 Reforms in Detail — Devaluation, Committees, Sector Reforms, Outcomes and Andhra Pradesh
items.body:
**In one line:** the 1991 rescue began with a **rupee devaluation** and an **IMF loan**, was carried forward by expert committees (Narasimham, Chelliah, Malhotra, Rangarajan), spread to telecom, power, digital payments and labour, and **Andhra Pradesh** became an early State-level reformer.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC 2017 asked which indicators rose or fell after 1991; "which committee → which sector" and "which reform → which year" are standard matching items; AP's power-sector unbundling is an AP-specific favourite.

## The first steps (1991-93)

**The story**

| Step | Detail |
|---|---|
| **IMF loan** | About **US$2.2 billion** (source text) with reform conditions |
| **Devaluation** | Rupee devalued in **two steps on 1 and 3 July 1991** (about 18-19% in all) |
| **New Industrial Policy** | **24 July 1991** — the same day as Manmohan Singh's first Budget |
| **LERMS** (Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System) | **March 1992** — a dual exchange rate |
| **Unified, market-determined rate** | **March 1993** |
| **Current-account convertibility** | **August 1994** |

## Objectives of the New Economic Policy

Reduce **inflation**, rebuild **foreign currency reserves**, raise **growth**, enlarge the **private sector's** role and **integrate** India with world markets.

## Committees that shaped the reforms

| Committee | Area |
|---|---|
| **Narasimham Committee I (1991)** and **II (1998)** | Banking — lower SLR/CRR, Basel norms, competition |
| **Raja Chelliah Committee (1991-93)** | Tax reform |
| **Malhotra Committee (1993-94)** | Opening **insurance** to private firms → **IRDA Act, 1999** |
| **C. Rangarajan Committee (1993)** | **Disinvestment** of PSEs |
| **Tarapore Committees (1997, 2006)** | Capital-account convertibility roadmap |

- The Department of Disinvestment (1999) was renamed **DIPAM** (Department of Investment and Public Asset Management) in **2016**.

## Reforms in other sectors (source table)

| Sector | Reform and year |
|---|---|
| Telecom | **New Telecom Policy, 1999**; **TRAI** (1997); NDCP **2018**; 5G roll-out (2022-23) |
| Power | **Electricity Act, 2003**; **UDAY** (2015) for DISCOM finances; National Solar Mission |
| Infrastructure | NHDP, **Bharatmala**, Smart Cities, **AMRUT (2015)** |
| Social | **RTE Act 2009**, **Ayushman Bharat (2018)**, MGNREGA |
| Labour | Code on Wages **2019**; Industrial Relations and Social Security Codes **2020** |
| Agriculture | APMC amendments, KCC, **PM-KISAN**, **e-NAM** |

## Digital reforms (source table)

| Reform | Year |
|---|---|
| **Aadhaar** | **2010** |
| **BharatNet** (National Optical Fibre Network) | **2011** |
| **Jan Dhan Yojana** | **2014** |
| **Digital India** | **2015** |
| **UPI**, **Start-up India**, GeM | **2016** |
| **ONDC** (Open Network for Digital Commerce) | **2022** |
| National Cyber Security Policy | **2013** |

## Outcomes after 1991 (UPSC 2017)

- **Rose:** India's share in world exports, **FDI inflows**, **foreign exchange reserves**.
- **Fell:** the **share of agriculture in GDP** — it did **not** rise.
- Sector impact (source): IT and services boomed; manufacturing grew unevenly; agriculture saw less public investment and costlier inputs.

## Andhra Pradesh — an early State reformer

| Reform | Detail |
|---|---|
| **AP Electricity Reform Act, 1998** | **APSEB** unbundled (1999) into **APGENCO** (generation) and **APTRANSCO** (transmission); **APERC** regulator set up |
| **Vision 2020** (1999) | Chandrababu Naidu government's long-term development plan |
| **World Bank loan (1998)** | **Andhra Pradesh Economic Restructuring Project** — a State-level reform loan |
| Today | **Swarna Andhra @2047** vision and the AP Industrial Development Policy 4.0 |

**Don't confuse** — *Narasimham* (banking) with *Malhotra* (insurance) and *Rangarajan* (disinvestment); *LERMS 1992* (dual rate) with the *1993* unified rate.

**TL;DR**
- IMF loan of about US$2.2 billion (source text); rupee devalued in two steps on 1 and 3 July 1991.
- New Industrial Policy announced on 24 July 1991; LERMS (dual rate) March 1992; unified market rate March 1993.
- NEP objectives: cut inflation, rebuild forex reserves, raise growth, enlarge the private sector, integrate with world markets.
- Narasimham Committees (1991, 1998) — banking; Malhotra Committee — insurance (IRDA Act 1999); C. Rangarajan Committee (1993) — disinvestment.
- Department of Disinvestment (1999) renamed DIPAM in 2016.

items.title: BoP Questions, Exchange Rates, Forex Reserves and External-Sector Instruments
items.body:
**In one line:** the current account holds trade, invisibles and remittances, the capital/financial account holds FDI, portfolio money and loans; the rupee's value is tracked by NEER/REER, and reserves are four assets — foreign currency, gold, SDRs and the IMF reserve tranche.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC asked current-account items (2014), capital-account items (2013), India's trade pattern (2020), what cuts currency-crisis risk (2019), P-Notes (2019) and convertibility (2015).

## Which account? (UPSC 2013-2014)

**The story**

| Item | Account |
|---|---|
| **Balance of trade** (goods) | Current |
| **Balance of invisibles** (services, income, transfers) | Current |
| **Private remittances** | **Current** (unilateral transfers) — **not** capital |
| **Foreign loans**, **FDI**, **portfolio investment** | **Capital / financial** |
| Foreign assets and **SDRs** | **Not** in the current account |

## India's trade pattern (UPSC 2020)

- **Merchandise exports < merchandise imports** — a trade deficit every year.
- **Services exports > services imports** — a services surplus (IT, business services).
- Overall a **current account deficit** in most years.
- **Remittances** and **IT export earnings** reduce the risk of a currency crisis; **more government spending** does not (UPSC 2019).
- India is the **world's largest recipient of remittances**.

## Worked example (source text, corrected)

Exports $500 bn, imports $700 bn, FDI inflow $100 bn, remittances $50 bn.

1. **Trade deficit** = 700 − 500 = **$200 bn**.
2. **Current account** = −200 + 50 (remittances are current) = **−$150 bn**.
3. **Financial account** = +$100 bn (FDI).
4. Shortfall of **$50 bn** must come from reserves or borrowing.

## BoP crisis — causes and consequences (source)

- **Causes:** high trade deficit, low reserves, excessive borrowing, policy mismanagement, global shocks (oil, wars).
- **Consequences:** **currency depreciation**, inflation and unemployment, **dependence on bailouts** (IMF).
- **Remedies:** export promotion, import substitution, reserve building, prudent fiscal policy.

## Exchange-rate words

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Devaluation** | Government/central bank **deliberately** lowers a **fixed** rate (India, July 1991) |
| **Depreciation** | **Market-driven** fall of a floating currency |
| **NEER** | Nominal Effective Exchange Rate — rupee against a **basket** of currencies; a rise = **appreciation** |
| **REER** | NEER **adjusted for inflation** differences |
| **Convertibility** | Freely converting the rupee into other currencies **and vice versa** (UPSC 2015) |

## Forex reserves

- Four parts: **Foreign Currency Assets** (largest), **gold**, **SDRs**, **Reserve Tranche Position** in the IMF.
- **Import cover** = months of imports the reserves can pay for (1991: about 3 weeks).
- India's reserves first crossed **US$700 billion** in **September 2024**.

## External-sector instruments

| Instrument | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Participatory Note (P-Note)** | Lets overseas investors buy Indian securities **without registering** with SEBI — issued by registered FPIs (UPSC 2019) |
| **Masala bond** | **Rupee-denominated** bond issued **abroad** — first by the **IFC** (World Bank arm); currency risk is borne by the investor |
| **ECB** | External Commercial Borrowing by Indian firms |
| **FPI limit** | A single FPI may hold below **10%** of a company; above that it counts as FDI |
| **GIFT City IFSC** | Gujarat — India's International Financial Services Centre, regulated by the **IFSCA (2020)** |

- **FDI vs FII** (UPSC 2011): FDI brings technology and management and is stable; FII adds general capital to markets and is volatile.

**AP link:** Andhra Pradesh's export earnings lean on **marine products (shrimp)** — AP is India's largest farmed-shrimp producer — so the rupee's exchange rate and US tariffs feed straight into AP's farm incomes.

**Don't confuse** — *devaluation* (policy act) with *depreciation* (market fall); *NEER* (nominal) with *REER* (inflation-adjusted); remittances (current) with FDI (financial).

**TL;DR**
- Current account includes the balance of trade and the balance of invisibles; foreign assets and SDRs are not current-account items (UPSC 2014).
- Capital account includes foreign loans, FDI and portfolio investment; private remittances are current account (UPSC 2013).
- India: merchandise exports < imports, services exports > imports, overall CAD (UPSC 2020).
- IT export earnings and remittances reduce currency-crisis risk; government spending does not (UPSC 2019).
- India is the world's largest recipient of remittances.

items.title: WTO in Depth — GATT to WTO, Ministerials, Agriculture Boxes, TFA, TRIPS and the Other Global Bodies
items.body:
**In one line:** GATT (1947) became the WTO (1995) after the Uruguay Round; Ministerial Conferences from Singapore (1996) to **Yaoundé (2026)** shaped the rules; the farm-subsidy "boxes", the Trade Facilitation Agreement and TRIPS are the parts India fights over.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC asked the boxes (2016), AoA/SPS/Peace Clause (2015), the TFA (2017), TRIMS (2020), the SDR basket (2016), AIIB (2019) and who publishes which report (2016, 2019).

## From GATT to WTO

**The story**

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| **1947** | **GATT** signed (in force 1948); India among the **23 founding** contracting parties |
| **1986-94** | **Uruguay Round** |
| **15 April 1994** | **Marrakesh Agreement** |
| **1 January 1995** | **WTO** begins; HQ **Geneva**; **166 members** |
| Director-General | **Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala** (since 2021) — first woman and first African DG |

## Ministerial Conferences (the top body)

| MC | Place and year | Remember |
|---|---|---|
| 1st | **Singapore 1996** | 'Singapore issues' (investment, competition, procurement, facilitation) |
| 4th | **Doha 2001** | **Doha Development Round**; Doha Declaration on TRIPS and public health |
| 9th | **Bali 2013** | **Trade Facilitation Agreement** + **Peace Clause** |
| 10th | **Nairobi 2015** | End of farm **export subsidies** |
| 12th | **Geneva 2022** | **Fisheries subsidies** agreement |
| 13th | **Abu Dhabi 2024** | — |
| 14th | **Yaoundé (Cameroon) 2026** | — |

## Agreement on Agriculture — the three boxes (UPSC 2016)

| Box | Type of subsidy | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **Amber** | **Trade-distorting** (price support, input subsidies) | **Capped** — measured as AMS |
| **Blue** | Amber-type but tied to **production limits** | Allowed |
| **Green** | **Minimal or no** distortion (research, food stocks, direct income support) | Allowed |

- **De minimis** limit: **10%** of production value for **developing** countries (5% for developed).
- **Peace Clause (Bali 2013)** protects India's public stockholding (MSP procurement) from challenge until a permanent solution.

## Other agreements

| Agreement | Fact |
|---|---|
| **TFA** (Trade Facilitation Agreement) | Part of the **Bali package (2013)**; India ratified it (2016); **in force February 2017** — not January 2016 (UPSC 2017) |
| **TRIMS** | Investment measures that affect **trade in goods only**; bans measures like **quantitative import restrictions** on foreign investors; does **not** regulate foreign investment itself (UPSC 2020) |
| **TRIPS** | Intellectual property; India's **Patents Act 1970** was amended in **2005** to allow **product patents**; **Section 3(d)** stops 'evergreening' (Novartis case, 2013); first **compulsory licence** — Natco for Bayer's Nexavar (2012) |
| **SPS** | Food safety and animal/plant health |

- **Dispute settlement:** the **Appellate Body** has not functioned since **December 2019** (no judges appointed).

## Other global economic bodies

| Body | Facts |
|---|---|
| **IMF** (Bretton Woods, 1944) | **SDR basket**: US dollar, euro, **Chinese renminbi (added 2016)**, yen, pound (UPSC 2016) |
| **World Bank** | IBRD (1944), IDA (1960), IFC (1956), MIGA (1988), ICSID (1966); **Ease of Doing Business** report (UPSC 2016) — discontinued **2021**, replaced by **B-READY** (2024) |
| **WEF** | **Global Competitiveness Report** (UPSC 2019) |
| **UNCTAD** (1964, Geneva) | **World Investment Report** |
| **AIIB** (2016, **Beijing**) | **China** the largest shareholder, **India the second**; has non-Asian members (UPSC 2019) |
| **NDB** (BRICS, 2015, **Shanghai**) | First president **K.V. Kamath** |

**AP link:** India's WTO defence of **public stockholding and MSP** protects States such as **Andhra Pradesh**, a leading paddy procurer for the central pool.

**Don't confuse** — *amber* (capped) with *green* (allowed); *TFA* (Bali 2013, in force 2017) with *Peace Clause* (Bali 2013, interim); *AIIB* (Beijing) with *NDB* (Shanghai).

**TL;DR**
- GATT 1947 (India among 23 founding parties); Uruguay Round 1986-94; Marrakesh Agreement 15 April 1994; WTO 1 January 1995.
- WTO DG Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala (since 2021) — first woman and first African DG; 166 members.
- Ministerials: Singapore 1996 (Singapore issues), Doha 2001 (Doha Round), Bali 2013 (TFA, Peace Clause), Nairobi 2015 (end export subsidies), Geneva 2022 (fisheries), Abu Dhabi 2024, Yaoundé 2026.
- Amber box = trade-distorting, capped (AMS); Blue box = production-limiting, allowed; Green box = minimal distortion, allowed (UPSC 2016).
- De minimis limit 10% for developing countries and 5% for developed.

items.title: India's Trade Agreements, Export Schemes, SEZs and US Tariffs — the 2026 Picture
items.body:
**In one line:** India now has trade deals with most of its big partners — UAE, Australia, EFTA, UK, Oman, New Zealand and (concluded) the **EU** — runs exports through RoDTEP, EPCG and SEZs, and faced a **50% US tariff** in 2025-26.

**Why it is asked:** "match the FTA with the partner/year", the EU deal ("mother of all trade deals", formerly BTIA — UPSC 2017), RCEP exit, SEZ firsts and the 2025 US tariffs are current-affairs staples.

## India's trade agreements — in force or concluded

**The story**

| Agreement | Partner | Signed | In force |
|---|---|---|---|
| **APTA** (Bangkok Agreement) | Asia-Pacific | 1975 | — |
| India–Sri Lanka FTA | Sri Lanka | 1998 | **2000** |
| **SAFTA** | SAARC | 2004 | **2006** |
| CECA | **Singapore** | 2005 | **2005** (India's first CECA) |
| ASEAN–India trade in goods | ASEAN | 2009 | **2010** |
| CEPA | **South Korea** | 2009 | 2010 |
| CEPA | **Japan** | 2011 | 2011 |
| CECPA | **Mauritius** | 2021 | 2021 (first with an African country) |
| CEPA | **UAE** | Feb 2022 | **1 May 2022** |
| ECTA | **Australia** | Apr 2022 | **29 Dec 2022** |
| **TEPA** | **EFTA** | **10 March 2024** | **1 Oct 2025** |
| **CETA** | **UK** | **24 Jul 2025** (Chequers) | **15 Jul 2026** |
| **CEPA** | **Oman** | **18 Dec 2025** | **1 Jun 2026** |
| **FTA** | **New Zealand** | **27 Apr 2026** | **20 Oct 2026** |
| **India–EU FTA** | European Union | Concluded **27 January 2026** | Pending |

- The **India–EU FTA** was earlier negotiated as the **BTIA** (Broad-based Trade and Investment Agreement — UPSC 2017); leaders called it the **"mother of all trade deals"**.
- **Under negotiation:** USA (bilateral trade agreement), Canada, Israel, Peru, Chile (CEPA), South Africa, Bangladesh.
- India **walked out of RCEP** in **November 2019** — fear of Chinese imports, dairy and a widening trade deficit.

## Export promotion tools

| Tool | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **RoDTEP** (Jan 2021) | Refunds embedded taxes on exports — replaced **MEIS** (WTO-incompatible) |
| **EPCG** | Duty-free import of capital goods against an export obligation |
| **Advance Authorisation** | Duty-free import of inputs used in exports |
| **Towns of Export Excellence** | Clusters with special support (FTP 2023 added more) |
| **Districts as Export Hubs** | FTP 2023 pillar — export plans for every district |
| FTP 2023 e-commerce | Courier export limit raised from **₹5 lakh to ₹10 lakh** per consignment |

## EPZs and SEZs

- **Kandla (1965)** — **Asia's first Export Processing Zone**.
- **Visakhapatnam** — one of the seven central-government EPZs, now the **Visakhapatnam SEZ (VSEZ)** at Duvvada.
- **SEZ Policy April 2000**; **SEZ Act, 2005** (rules 2006); **Export Oriented Units** scheme 1981.
- **Sri City** (Tirupati district) is a large private multi-product SEZ on the AP–Tamil Nadu border.

## US tariffs, 2025-26

- From **27 August 2025** most Indian goods faced a **50% US tariff** — a 25% 'reciprocal' tariff plus a **25% penalty for buying Russian oil**.
- The 25% penalty was **withdrawn in February 2026**.
- **AP link:** shrimp is AP's biggest farm export and the US is its main market, so the 50% tariff hit **Andhra Pradesh aqua farmers** hardest among States.

**Don't confuse** — *TEPA* (EFTA: Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein) with the *EU FTA*; *CEPA UAE (2022)* with *CEPA Oman (2026)*; *Kandla* (first EPZ) with *Santacruz SEEPZ* (electronics EPZ).

**TL;DR**
- India–EU FTA concluded on 27 January 2026 ("mother of all trade deals"); it was earlier negotiated as the BTIA (UPSC 2017).
- India–Oman CEPA: signed 18 December 2025, in force 1 June 2026.
- India–New Zealand FTA: signed 27 April 2026, in force 20 October 2026.
- India–UK CETA signed 24 July 2025 at Chequers, in force 15 July 2026; India–EFTA TEPA in force 1 October 2025.
- SAFTA in force 2006; India–Sri Lanka FTA 2000; Singapore CECA 2005; ASEAN goods 2010; South Korea CEPA 2010; Japan CEPA 2011; Mauritius CECPA 2021.

items.title: FDI and FPI in Detail — Agencies, Caps, FPI Categories, Trends and Promotion Steps
items.body:
**In one line:** FDI policy is made by **DPIIT**, foreign exchange is regulated by the **RBI under FEMA**, portfolio money by **SEBI**; caps now allow **100% in insurance** (December 2025), 74% automatic in defence and 26% in digital news, and net FDI has slumped as foreign firms repatriate profits.

**Why it is asked:** caps and their latest changes, "which body regulates whom", FPI categories and the Survey's FDI trends are frequently tested.

## Agencies

**The story**

| Agency | Role |
|---|---|
| **DPIIT** (Ministry of Commerce and Industry) | FDI policy and promotion |
| **RBI** | Foreign exchange under **FEMA, 1999** |
| **SEBI** | FPIs under the **SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019** — which **merged FIIs, sub-accounts and QFIs into FPIs** |
| **FIPB** | Cleared approval-route FDI — **abolished 2017**; now the ministries concerned decide |
| Ministry of Finance | Taxation of foreign investment |

## Sector caps — the current list

| Sector | Cap |
|---|---|
| **Insurance** | **100%** — **Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025** (December 2025); history 26% (2000) → 49% (2014) → 74% (2021) |
| **Defence** | **74% automatic**, up to 100% with approval |
| **Telecom** | 100% |
| **Single-brand retail** | 100% automatic |
| **E-commerce marketplace model** | 100% (inventory model not allowed) |
| **Digital news media** | **26%** with government approval |
| **Renewable energy** | 100% automatic |

- **Press Note 3 (April 2020):** FDI from countries **sharing a land border** with India (e.g. China) needs **government approval**.

## FPI categories and limits (source text)

- **Category I** — governments, central banks, sovereign wealth funds, multilateral bodies.
- **Category II** — mutual funds, banks, insurers, asset managers.
- **Category III** — others (HNIs, family offices). *(SEBI's 2019 rules actually use **two** categories — the source text's three-way split is the older scheme.)*
- A single FPI may hold **less than 10%** of a company; total foreign holding must stay within the sectoral cap.

## Trends (Economic Survey 2023-24 and after)

- **Global FDI** fell **2%** to **US$1.3 trillion** in 2023 (UNCTAD).
- India's FDI plus portfolio inflows ≈ **2.5% of GDP** a year over two decades (IMF).
- **Net FDI**: **US$42 bn (FY23) → US$26.5 bn (FY24)**; gross inflows fell only 0.6%. Net FDI kept shrinking in 2024-25 because of **repatriation** and **outward FDI** by Indian firms.
- **Digital FDI** share: **46.6% (FY17) → 69.2% (FY21)**.
- **Top sources:** **Singapore**, **Mauritius**, USA.

## Promotion steps

- **Make in India (2014)**, Start-up India, **PLI** schemes, **National Single Window System**, industrial corridors (**DMIC**, Chennai–Bengaluru), SEZs, corporate tax of **15%** for new manufacturing firms, Bilateral Investment Treaties.

**AP link:** the **Chennai–Bengaluru** and **Visakhapatnam–Chennai** industrial corridors pass through **Andhra Pradesh** (for example the Krishnapatnam node), which is why AP pitches itself to FDI investors; AP also hosts PLI-linked electronics units at Sri City and Tirupati.

**Don't confuse** — *insurance 100%* (December 2025) with *defence 74%* (automatic); *SEBI* (FPI) with *DPIIT* (FDI policy) and *RBI* (FEMA).

**TL;DR**
- Insurance FDI cap raised to 100% by the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025 (December 2025); earlier 26% → 49% (2014) → 74% (2021).
- Defence 74% automatic (100% with approval); telecom, single-brand retail and e-commerce marketplace 100%; digital news media 26% with approval.
- SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019 merged FIIs, sub-accounts and QFIs into FPIs.
- FIPB abolished in 2017; DPIIT frames FDI policy; RBI regulates forex under FEMA 1999.
- Press Note 3 (April 2020): FDI from land-border countries needs government approval.

items.title: For Mains — Economic Reforms, Foreign Trade & WTO
items.body:
## In one line

For Mains, this topic is a debate on **openness vs protection**: did liberalisation and global trade integration deliver inclusive growth, and how should India balance WTO rules with food security and strategic autonomy? (Serves mains-4 clauses M4-1, M4-2 and M4-9.)

## The dimensions Mains asks

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Causes | 1991 BoP crisis, twin deficits, IMF conditionality |
| Features | LPG pillars, FEMA, FTP 2023, WTO agreements, FTAs |
| Significance | Higher growth, IT/services boom, FDI, global value chains |
| Impact | Jobless/uneven growth, agrarian stress, trade-deficit worries |
| Criticism / limits | WTO AoA vs MSP, RCEP exit, FTA concessions |
| Way forward | Second-generation reforms, export diversification, update AoA |

## Data / committees / reports to quote

- **1991:** forex ~US$1.2 bn (2–3 weeks' imports); gold pledge; Narasimham Committee (banking).
- **FDI (Economic Survey 2023-24):** net FDI fell US$42 bn (FY23) → US$26.5 bn (FY24); caps — insurance 74%, defence 74% auto.
- **FTP 2023:** US$2 trillion export target by 2030 (DGFT).
- **FTAs live (Oct 2026):** UAE CEPA (2022), Australia ECTA (2022), **EFTA TEPA (1 Oct 2025, US$100 bn pledge)**, **UK CETA (in force 15 Jul 2026)**; RCEP exit 2019.
- **WTO:** Bali Peace Clause (2013); AoA de minimis 10% on 1986-88 prices.

## AP angle

Liberalisation lifted **AP's IT/pharma and Visakhapatnam port-led industry**, but its farm-dependent economy stays exposed to global price swings; FTAs matter for AP's **seafood and pharma exports**.

## Use in answers

- **Example:** cite the UK CETA (2026) and EFTA TEPA as India's new-generation, investment-linked FTAs.
- **Quote:** reforms were 'growth-enhancing but not sufficiently employment-generating'.
- **Diagram idea:** a timeline from 1991 LPG → WTO 1995 → FTP 2023 → CETA 2026.
keyPoints: Mains frames this as openness vs protection and inclusive growth (M4-1, M4-2, M4-9).
Use the dimensions table: causes, features, significance, impact, criticism, way forward.
Quote 1991 forex ~US$1.2 bn, FDI FY24 US$26.5 bn, FTP 2023 US$2 tn target, live FTAs, Bali Peace Clause.
Key tensions: WTO AoA vs MSP food stockholding; RCEP exit; FTA concessions.
AP angle: IT/pharma/ports gained; farm economy exposed; FTAs aid seafood/pharma exports.
